title: Unemployment in India
tagline: What unemployment means, its three prescribed types — seasonal, structural, technological — its causes, and the schemes built against it.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Economics syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (the 2026-27 session syllabus as reproduced by Shaalaa and Jagran Josh; the official cisce.org PDFs were not retrievable). Every question and answer is original practice, no board examination paper was consulted, and no figure is presented as an official statistic.

overview.intro: Unemployment is the second of the syllabus’s major problems, and unlike poverty it has a crisp definition: a person able and willing to work at the going wage, actively seeking work, and not finding it. From that definition the syllabus builds outward in its own fixed order — meaning first, then the three prescribed types with a meaning and an example each, then any five causes, and finally the government schemes introduced against unemployment and poverty, two of which must be studied with their objectives. The three types are the analytical core, because each identifies a different mechanism: the calendar (seasonal), the structure of the economy (structural), and the machine (technological). The causes explain why the problem persists at scale, and the schemes close the syllabus by matching instruments to those causes — which is exactly how the final questions in this chapter are built.

learningOutcomes: Classify situations into seasonal, structural or technological unemployment with justification.
State and explain at least five causes of unemployment.
Describe at least two government schemes with their objectives.
Relate each scheme to the cause it treats.

blocks.text: Unemployment exists when a person who is able to work, willing to work at the prevailing wage, and actively looking for work does not get any. All three conditions matter and each one excludes something. Ability excludes those genuinely unable to work; willingness at the going wage excludes a person demanding an unreasonable price for labour — that is a refusal to work rather than unemployment; and actively seeking excludes those who have stopped looking, whose idleness is real but who fall outside the count until they search again. The definition is therefore about a mismatch in a market: supply of labour is offered, demand exists somewhere, and the two do not meet. Why they fail to meet is what the rest of the chapter studies — because the reasons can sit in the calendar, in the structure of the economy, or in the technology itself, and each reason implies a different remedy. A last distinction keeps the term honest: unemployment counts people with no work at all, and the syllabus’s types explain the forms that no-work takes — periodically, persistently, or as a result of displacement — without ever being a synonym for low income or hard luck.

items: Able: the person is capable of doing available work.
Willing at the going wage: ready to accept work at the price employers actually pay.
Actively seeking: looking, registering or applying — the condition that puts a person in the count.
Not finding: the mismatch between the labour offered and the jobs available.
The three types each explain a different reason for the same mismatch: calendar, structure, technology.

learn.title: The three prescribed types: seasonal, structural, technological

blocks.text: Seasonal unemployment follows the calendar. In an agriculture-dominated economy, work concentrates in the crop cycle — planting, weeding and harvesting demand heavy labour, and between harvest and the next sowing there is too little to do, so the same labourer is employed for part of the year and idle for the rest. The example is the standard one: a landless farm worker with six months of work in the fields and no alternative occupation in the slack months, whose income arrives in blocks with a hunger gap in between. Structural unemployment arises from the structure of the economy itself: the economy generates fewer jobs than there are people seeking them, because too small an industrial and service base cannot absorb the workforce, or because production is organised with a skill or capital requirement that large numbers of workers do not meet. The example: an economy where the number of job-seekers in a district far exceeds the posts its firms can offer, so every vacancy draws a queue — unemployment persisting even when people are willing to work. Technological unemployment is displacement by machinery: when a firm substitutes machines for workers, output may rise while headcount falls, and the replaced workers are unemployed until they find employers who still need their skill. The example is the classic one — powerlooms and automatic machinery replacing handloom weavers, or bank machines replacing routine clerical work. The three are told apart by cause, not by severity: seasonal ends when the season turns, structural ends when the economy’s structure changes, technological ends when displaced workers are reabsorbed or retrained — and an answer that names a type without stating its cause has not actually classified anything.

learn.title: Why unemployment persists: the prescribed causes

blocks.text: The syllabus asks for any five causes, and the standard set moves from the population side of the market to the job side and then to the fit between them. Rapid population growth adds entrants to the labour market every year faster than the economy creates vacancies, so even an economy that is creating jobs can leave the queue undiminished — the denominator of the problem grows continuously. Slow growth of employment opportunities is the mirror cause: industry and services expand too slowly to absorb the workforce, and where growth is capital-intensive it raises output without raising headcount proportionately, producing jobs by investment far below the rate workers need. The seasonal nature of agriculture — already visible in the seasonal type — is a cause at the national scale: a monsoon-dependent, calendar-bound sector employing the majority guarantees a large pool of under-used labour through the lean months. Defective education and training is the mismatch cause: what schools and colleges teach does not match what employers buy, so vacancies and job-seekers coexist side by side — employers cannot fill posts while applicants cannot find them. The shift to technology and capital-intensive methods displaces existing workers faster than new work appears in adjacent sectors, converting employed into unemployed in a single investment decision. Unequal distribution of land concentrates the rest: where holdings shrink through inheritance and landless labour multiplies, too many people depend on plots too small to employ them. Each cause names its own remedy, which is why the schemes at the end of the chapter are studied against this list rather than on their own.

items.meaning: Labour-market entrants outnumbering vacancies created each year.
items.context: Population growth keeps unemployment rising even while jobs are being created.

items.meaning: Industry and services expanding too slowly, or capital-intensively, to absorb workers.
items.context: Output can grow faster than headcount when growth is capital-intensive.

items.meaning: The crop cycle that concentrates work into part of the year.
items.context: A monsoon-dependent sector employing the majority guarantees a lean-month labour pool.

items.meaning: Qualifications held by job-seekers differing from what employers need.
items.context: A mismatch lets vacancies and unemployment exist simultaneously.

items.meaning: Workers replaced by machines in a single investment decision.
items.context: Displacement converts the employed into the unemployed without any fall in output.

items.meaning: Holdings divided by inheritance until they cannot employ their holders.
items.context: Fragmentation creates disguised dependence on plots too small to support them.

learn.title: Schemes and programmes against unemployment and poverty

blocks.text: The syllabus requires two programmes to be studied with their objectives, drawn from its illustrative list — IRDP, JRY, PKVY, HRIDAY, MNREGA and others — and the two best chosen for how directly they answer the causes are MNREGA and IRDP. The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act guarantees wage employment: every rural household whose adult volunteer performs unskilled manual work is entitled to work for a hundred days in a year, on locally useful assets — roads, canals, ponds, watershed works — with the work created on demand rather than offered by schedule. Its objectives are precise: to provide an employment floor that eliminates distress migration and calender-driven hunger, to create durable assets that raise the village’s future productivity, and to place a legal floor under rural wages. The scheme maps onto the seasonal cause directly — it fills exactly the lean months when the fields have nothing to offer. The Integrated Rural Development Programme attacks the other side: it assists rural families below the poverty line to acquire productive assets — dairy animals, equipment, tools for a trade — through a combination of government subsidy and bank credit, so that the household becomes self-employed rather than waiting for a wage. Its objective is income creation through assets: employment that continues past the scheme, financed rather than granted, which is why it also depends on the banking network. Other programmes on the list work on adjacent gaps — wage employment through panchayati-rural works, skill and heritage-linked development — but the examination rule is simple: any two, each with objectives stated and mechanisms clear. The analytical closing point is that schemes answer causes: a wage guarantee answers the calendar, self-employment finance answers the absence of jobs, and neither substitutes for the structural cause of too few posts — which only faster, job-creating growth can move.

items.text: In the months between harvest and sowing, a rural household earns wages building a village check dam under the employment guarantee.
items.note: The lean season converted into income — and the dam remains as an asset afterwards.

items.text: A landless family receives a subsidy-cum-credit package to buy two milch animals and sells milk daily thereafter.
items.note: IRDP’s objective in one line: an asset that keeps generating income after the scheme ends.

keyPoints: Unemployment = able + willing at the going wage + actively seeking + not finding.
The definition excludes non-searchers and unreasonable wage demands — it is a market mismatch, not hardship generally.
Seasonal unemployment follows the crop calendar; it ends when the season turns.
Structural unemployment: the economy generates fewer jobs than seekers — structure, not unwillingness.
Technological unemployment: machines replace workers; output can rise while headcount falls.
Classify by cause, not severity — a type named without its cause is not classified.
Causes: population growth, slow job creation, agriculture’s calendar, training mismatch, technology shift, land fragmentation.
Vacancies and unemployment coexist when the training mismatch is wide.
MNREGA: 100 days of guaranteed rural wage work on local assets — the lean season answered directly.
IRDP: subsidy plus credit to acquire productive assets — self-employment rather than a waiting wage.
Schemes answer causes; only job-creating growth answers the structural cause.
examFocus: State the definition with all four conditions — each one excludes a case the examiner is checking for.
Classify every example by naming the type and then the cause in the same breath.
Keep to the three prescribed types — seasonal, structural, technological — with a meaning and an example each.
Causes must be chains: condition → mechanism → consequence, at least five.
Scheme answers state objectives explicitly — what the programme is trying to achieve, not only what it does.
Map scheme to cause: wage guarantee answers the calendar; asset finance answers missing jobs.
Close by naming what schemes cannot do — the structural cause needs job-creating growth.
Use concrete examples: lean-season farm labour, powerloom displacement, hundred days of rural work.

questions.prompt: A farm labourer works at sowing and harvest and finds no work between harvest and the next sowing. This is:
questions.explanation: The idleness follows the crop calendar — work concentrated in parts of the year with a regular slack period. It ends when the season turns, which distinguishes it from the persistent forms.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it disguised unemployment — the prescribed type for calendar-bound work in this syllabus is seasonal.

questions.prompt: Powerlooms replacing handloom weavers is the standard example of:
questions.explanation: Machines substituted for workers displace labour even while output rises — the defining mechanism of technological unemployment, unlike calendar or structural causes.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it structural: structural means too few jobs in the economy’s shape, not jobs lost to a specific machine.

questions.prompt: Why can vacancies and unemployment exist at the same time?
options: Training mismatch: applicants lack the skills the open posts require
The wage demanded is above the legal minimum everywhere
Unemployment is counted only in cities
questions.answer: Training mismatch: applicants lack the skills the open posts require
questions.explanation: Defective education and training let unfilled posts sit beside job-seekers who cannot qualify for them — a fit problem rather than a shortage of either jobs or workers.
questions.commonMistake: Answering “there are not enough jobs” — that is the structural cause and cannot explain simultaneous vacancies.

questions.prompt: The primary objective of a guaranteed rural wage-employment scheme is to:
options: Provide a work floor so households survive the lean season without distress migration
Raise interest rates on farm loans
questions.answer: Provide a work floor so households survive the lean season without distress migration
questions.explanation: The guarantee answers the calendar directly: wages when the fields offer nothing, ending the hunger gap and the migration it forces, while leaving durable local assets behind.
questions.commonMistake: Describing asset creation as the primary aim — assets are the method; the objective is the employment floor.

questions.prompt: Complete: ________ unemployment follows the crop calendar, ________ unemployment arises because the economy generates fewer jobs than seekers, and technological unemployment arises when machines replace workers.
questions.explanation: The three prescribed types are told apart by cause — calendar, structure and machine — and the first two blanks are the calendar and structure mechanisms.
questions.commonMistake: Swapping seasonal and structural: the calendar is timing; structure is the economy generating too few jobs.

questions.answer: Unemployment is the condition of a person who is able to work, willing to work at the prevailing wage, actively seeking work, and yet does not get any. Ability excludes those genuinely unable to work; willingness at the going wage excludes someone demanding an unreasonable price for labour; active search is what places the person in the count; and not finding work is the mismatch between the labour offered and the jobs available. The definition therefore describes a market mismatch rather than hardship in general, and the types of unemployment that follow each explain a different reason for the same mismatch.
questions.explanation: Full marks require all four conditions with one line each — the examiner is checking that the boundary cases (unwilling, not searching, unable) are excluded deliberately.
questions.commonMistake: A one-line “person without a job” definition, which accidentally counts retirees and those refusing the going wage.

questions.prompt: State the three types of unemployment with an example of each.
questions.answer: Seasonal unemployment follows the crop calendar: work is concentrated at sowing, weeding and harvest, and the landless farm worker finds no field work between harvest and the next sowing — idleness that ends when the season turns. Structural unemployment arises because the economy generates fewer jobs than there are seekers: in a district where the few firms offer posts far outnumbered by applicants, willing workers queue regardless of season — persistence built into the economy’s structure. Technological unemployment occurs when machines replace workers: powerlooms and automatic machinery displace handloom weavers and automated systems replace routine clerical work, leaving the displaced unemployed even as output rises.
questions.explanation: Three types with the cause and a concrete example each earn full marks; stating the cause is what distinguishes classification from listing.
questions.commonMistake: Giving examples without causes — the marks lie in showing why each situation is its type.

questions.prompt: Explain any five causes of unemployment.
questions.answer: Rapid population growth adds workers to the labour market every year at a rate above job creation, so the queue of seekers grows even while the economy is creating posts — the denominator of unemployment expands continuously. Slow growth of employment opportunities is the mirror side: industry and services expand too slowly to absorb the workforce, and where expansion is capital-intensive, output rises without a proportional rise in headcount, so investment creates jobs far below the rate workers need. The seasonal nature of agriculture operates as a national-scale cause: in a monsoon-dependent economy where the majority lives off the land, work is concentrated into parts of the year, guaranteeing a large pool of under-used labour in the slack months. Defective education and training creates the mismatch cause: what institutions teach does not match what employers buy, so vacancies and job-seekers coexist — unfilled posts beside unqualified applicants. The shift to technology and capital-intensive methods displaces existing workers faster than adjacent sectors absorb them, converting the employed into the unemployed in a single investment decision. Unequal distribution of land compounds all of the above: as holdings fragment through inheritance, too many people become dependent on plots too small to employ them. The causes interlock — population pressure widens the low-skill pool, low skill locks workers into casual work, technology removes even that, and agriculture’s calendar caps how much of the year any of it can run — which is why single-measure remedies leave the count largely unchanged.
questions.explanation: Five causes with mechanisms, plus the closing interlock paragraph, carry the full marks — headings without mechanisms earn only partial credit for “to be discussed”.
questions.commonMistake: Listing “poverty” as a cause of unemployment — it is largely an effect, and the syllabus’s cause list runs the other way.

questions.prompt: Describe two government schemes to remove unemployment and state their objectives.
questions.answer: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act is a wage-employment scheme: every rural household whose adult volunteers perform unskilled manual work is entitled to work for a hundred days per year, with employment provided on demand rather than on a schedule, on locally useful assets such as rural roads, canals, ponds and watershed works. Its objectives are threefold. To provide an employment floor — an income in the lean agricultural months so that no household is forced into the distress migration or hunger that the calendar otherwise imposes; to build durable assets whose productivity outlasts the wages paid for them, so the village is left better irrigated and better connected; and to place a legal floor under rural wages, which raises the bargaining position of landless labour even where no guarantee work is running. The scheme answers the seasonal and low-wage causes directly. The Integrated Rural Development Programme works on the other side: it assists rural families below the poverty line to acquire productive assets — milch animals, equipment, tools for a small trade — through a combination of government subsidy and bank credit, so that the household becomes self-employed instead of waiting for a wage to appear. Its objectives are income creation through ownership rather than through relief: employment that continues after the scheme ends, capital that belongs to the household, and the discipline of a business that must service its credit — which is why the programme runs through banks rather than through treasuries. Together the pair covers the two faces of the problem: the guarantee supplies work when the economy has none, while the asset scheme reduces dependence on wage work altogether. Neither, it should be stated honestly, resolves the structural cause — the economy generating fewer posts than seekers — because a guarantee cannot create permanent jobs in industry and services; that needs faster job-creating growth, which is the cause the schemes leave to the wider economy.
questions.explanation: Two schemes with objectives stated as objectives (floor, assets, income) rather than descriptions, plus the honest boundary statement about the structural cause, together make the complete answer the syllabus demands.
questions.commonMistake: Writing what the schemes do without naming objectives, or claiming a scheme “solves unemployment” when the structural cause is untouched.

questions.prompt: Match each prescribed cause of unemployment to the instrument that answers it, and identify the cause no instrument fully answers.
questions.answer: The matching discipline starts from the mechanism of each cause. Agriculture’s calendar creates lean-month idleness, and the direct answer is guaranteed rural wage work: employment created on demand during exactly the months the fields reject, converting dead time into income while leaving assets behind — the match is calendar to floor. The absence of jobs in places where people live is answered by self-employment finance: subsidy and credit for productive assets let a household create its own post rather than queue for someone else’s, so the match is missing jobs to asset creation. The training mismatch requires education and skill training aligned to what employers buy — the instrument must change the applicant rather than the vacancy, because the vacancy already exists unfilled. Land fragmentation and disguised dependence are partially answered by rural employment programmes and rural infrastructure, which raise the earning capacity of land that is too small to employ its holders on its own. Population growth is not an employment instrument at all — it is addressed by the slow-acting levers of education and family welfare, and its labour-market effect only fades when job creation outpaces entrants. The cause no instrument fully answers is the structural one: the economy generating fewer jobs than seekers. A wage guarantee supplies work but does not create a permanent post; asset finance creates self-employment at the household scale but cannot build an industrial base; training fits workers to vacancies that still must be created by somebody’s investment. Only faster growth that is itself job-creating — labour-using rather than purely capital-using — reduces the structural count, and even that depends on which sectors grow. The honest conclusion is therefore layered: instruments manage the seasonal, mismatch and subsistence faces well, they soften technology’s displacement through retraining, and they leave the structural core to the growth strategy itself — which is why unemployment figures improve only when all three layers move together.
questions.explanation: Full marks require an explicit mapping for at least four cause-instrument pairs with the logic of each match, the identification of the structural cause as the unanswerable one, and a layered conclusion; a flat list of schemes without matching stays at recall level.
questions.commonMistake: Treating every cause as equally solvable by schemes — the analytical point is precisely that one cause escapes them.
